newsitem.title: MEXICO: TV Azteca IPO finds receptive audience.
newsitem.headline: TV Azteca IPO finds receptive audience.

text.p: Mexican broadcaster TV Azteca Friday launched the largest initial public offering by a Mexican company since the 1994-95 peso crisis, tapping stock markets successfully only four years after its privatization.
Azteca sold 18.5 percent of the company for a total of $526 million in a global offering in Mexico, the United States and Europe. That meant the company overall was valued at $2.85 billion.

Investors eager to get a slice of one of Mexico's premier private companies gave a warm welcome to the company, driving up its share price 94 cents to $19.19 on the New York Stock Exchange in the stock's first day of action. "This is to make better TV in Mexico, better programs, better newscasts," Azteca majority owner Ricardo Salinas Pliego said during a live broadcast on his network from the floor of the Mexican stock market.
Azteca's 345,998,013 shares carried an initial offer price of $18.25 per American Depositary Shares (ADS) on the NYSE and 35.432 pesos per ordinary CPO share on the Mexican market.
Each CPO was made up of three shares and each ADS was worth four CPOs.

On the Mexican market, traders scrambled to buy Azteca stock as soon as it was placed, driving up the price to 38.20 pesos before sellers stepped in, and lowered it to 36.95 pesos in early afternoon trade.
"You know the way it goes, there was a lot of pushing and shoving to buy it to begin with, and then they lower their bids," one trader said.
"It was the day's big news. The word is it's a good long-term buy," another dealer said.
The company was only going to take in some $50 million from the primary offering, just 9 percent of the total.
Analysts said the remainder of the money was mostly going to the Saba family, Azteca's minority shareholders, who decided to sell their shares due to a reported split with Salinas Pliego.
Salinas Pliego, who owns 66 percent of the company, did not put up any of his shares for sale and denies he and the Sabas were at odds over the company's management.
Azteca lowered the amount of shares on offer this week, but bumped up the initial offer price from $15-$17 to $17-$19 -- a move which analysts said paid off.
"This was clearly a successful offer. And why not? Azteca has revolutionized Mexican television," one Mexico City analyst said.

Since it was privatized, the broadcaster has gobbled up market share from its larger rival, Grupo Televisa SA, at a much faster pace than expected, tripling its share of the television advertising market to 33 percent.
Azteca has used U.S.-style programming and lower ad rates to hurt the opposition.
